analysis.one_liner: Bans Members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House floor vote: after being introduced in February 2022 and sent to four committees, no committee ever acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit Members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading stocks, bonds, commodities, futures, or other securities, including hedge fund and derivative interests. Current members would have 180 days after the law takes effect to sell off these holdings; new members would have 180 days after taking office, and assets received mid-service (like an inheritance) would have to be sold within 180 days. Members could still own widely held, diversified mutual funds, government retirement plans, Treasury bonds, and small-business interests that pose no conflict of interest, and a spouse could keep trading assets used in their own separate job. Violations could bring a civil fine of up to $50,000 each, and members who had to sell would not owe capital-gains tax on the sale if they reinvested in permitted holdings within 60 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens benefit from lawmakers who no longer hold individual stocks while voting on bills, regulations, and subsidies that move those companies' prices. The prohibition removes the built-in conflict where a member can personally profit from legislation they write — for example, on defense contracts, drug prices, or energy rules. Members themselves with clean finances also gain, in the form of public trust they cannot otherwise buy back.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, and members without stock conflicts

how_it_helps.text: It bans ownership of and trading in individual stocks, bonds, commodities, futures, and securities — including hedge funds, derivatives, and options — by Members of Congress and their spouses, so lawmakers cannot personally hold or trade the very companies whose fate they decide.

Current members would have to divest within 180 days of enactment, new members within 180 days of being sworn in, and assets like inheritances received while in office within 180 days of receipt — closing the main ways members currently come to hold conflicting assets.

Violations carry a civil penalty of up to $50,000 per violation, enforceable by the Attorney General or Special Counsel in federal court, putting real legal consequences behind the ban rather than leaving it to congressional self-policing alone.

Members forced to sell would not owe capital-gains tax on those divestitures if they reinvest in permitted holdings within 60 days, removing the tax penalty that would otherwise make honest compliance costly.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses who hold individual stocks, hedge fund stakes, or other securities pay directly: they must sell those holdings on a fixed timetable and put the money into diversified funds or Treasury bonds. Wealthy members with large portfolios bear the largest adjustment. The general public pays nothing; the tax deferral provision has a negligible cost to the Treasury.

drawbacks.text: The $50,000 maximum fine per violation is small compared with the money at stake in congressional trading scandals, so a member who expected to profit by more than that could treat the penalty as a cost of doing business.

The bill leaves real loopholes: a spouse may keep trading securities used in the course of their own primary occupation, and assets received as compensation from a spouse's occupation are exempt — which a member with a well-timed family arrangement could use to keep market exposure in the household.

Members get up to five years to divest hedge fund, venture capital, and other privately held complex investments, the hardest-to-value holdings where conflicts are least visible, so the most opaque assets would linger longest.

Enforcement depends on the Attorney General or Special Counsel bringing civil suits, and on the House and Senate Ethics Committees writing the interpretive rules — bodies whose willingness to act against their own colleagues is exactly what critics of congressional self-policing question.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — removing the conflict of interest where lawmakers personally hold stocks while writing laws affecting those companies — is significant and the cost falls almost entirely on the members themselves. The bill is not airtight: the fine is modest, the spousal-occupation exemption leaves a route to keep household market exposure, and the slow five-year clock for private fund stakes protects the most opaque assets. But those are design imperfections in a reform whose core would plainly serve the public, and none of them changes who wins and who loses under it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees when introduced, none of them ever took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 — it never came to a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Representative Pramila Jayapal, a Democrat, introduced the bill on February 9, 2022 together with Representative Matt Rosendale, a Republican — the pairing behind the word 'Bipartisan' in its title.

The same day, the Speaker referred it to four committees at once — Financial Services, Agriculture, House Administration, and Ways and Means — a routing that meant any of them could have claimed jurisdiction and none had to act.
Two weeks later, on February 24, 2022, part of the bill was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Commodity Exchanges, Energy, and Credit — the last recorded action it ever received.
No committee held a markup, no vote was ever scheduled in the House or Senate, and the bill died with the Congress on January 3, 2023.

The bill would have required members and spouses to divest individual stocks and securities within 180 days, with a $50,000 civil fine per violation and tax-deferred rollovers into permitted investments.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress who hold individual stocks and securities are better off: they kept the ability to own and trade companies whose industries they regulate and fund, and no penalty or divestment clock ever started. The public got nothing from the bill's death except the continuation of the conflict it would have removed.

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban congressional stock ownership and trading on February 9, 2022.

for.name: Rep. Matt Rosendale
for.what_they_did: Joined Jayapal as the bill's Republican sponsor at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from day one.

for.name: 14 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining the sponsor in support.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House floor calendar in the 117th Congress and never brought this bill, or any congressional stock-trading ban, to a floor vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Chairs of the four committees of referral (Financial Services, Agriculture, House Administration, Ways and Means)
against.role: Committee chairs with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration in any of the four committees to which it was referred; no markup or committee vote occurred before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat (Jayapal) and a Republican (Rosendale) introduced it together, and the 15 cosponsors split 14 Democrats and 1 Republican — but no party ever brought it to a vote, so no roll call exists to measure where the parties actually stood.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their spouses holding individual stocks and securities
industries.note: Because no committee acted and the bill died, members kept the ability to own and trade individual companies while voting on the legislation, subsidies, and regulations that move those companies' prices. The status quo this bill would have ended is precisely what its supporters identified as a conflict of interest.

industries.industry: Brokerage and wealth-management firms serving congressional clients
industries.note: A ban would have pushed members' portfolios out of individual securities and into diversified funds and Treasury bonds, shifting where congressional money is invested. Members would still have been allowed to hold widely held diversified funds, so passive fund managers would have kept the business.
